articles.title: Bank of America fined $1.2bn over failing to stop money laundering
articles.summary: The bank inadequately flagged transactions linked to potential Chinese money laundering networks, the Treasury said.
articles.body:
Bank of America has been fined $1.2bn (£910m) for failing to detect potential money laundering and other illegal activity, the US Treasury Department said on Tuesday.

The banking giant failed to report over $5bn in suspicious activity to the government, $1bn of which posed national security and illicit finance risks, the Treasury said.

Those failures included not flagging transactions that possibly involved Chinese money laundering networks or trade-based laundering "with a substantial nexus to the southwest border", according to the Treasury.

"Our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators," Bank of America told the BBC.

The announcement came less 24 hours before Bank of America was due to announce its quarterly earnings on Wednesday morning.

"Our third-quarter results will include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share," the bank said in an emailed statement.

"We have already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base," it added.

In announcing the fine, the third-largest the department has ever imposed, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks."

The Treasury said the bank overly relied on inquiries from outside parties like law enforcement and other financial institutions instead of its own internal controls.

This meant that it "effectively outsourced to third parties a substantial portion of its proactive detection and reporting obligations," the department said.

As part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it "willfully violated" the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain a compliant anti-money laundering programme, conduct required due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts and file suspicious activity reports, the Treasury said.

The $1.2bn fine included penalties imposed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).

The OCC's $750m fine marked the biggest penalty it has ever levied.

OFAC said its settlement with the bank was tied to 475 apparent violations of sanctions programmes including those on Russia and Iran, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The settlement amount of $11.6m reflected the determination that Bank of America's apparent violations were "non-egregious", OFAC said.

articles.title: UN Human Rights Council elects 15 members in uncontested vote
articles.summary: Rights groups say uncontested vote undermines accountability as countries with poor human rights records win seats.
articles.body:
Human rights groups have sharply criticised the uncontested election of 15 members of the United Nations’ premier human rights body, saying it let countries with poor rights records win seats.

The 193-member General Assembly held the vote on Tuesday.

Positions on the 47-nation Human Rights Council are allocated to the UN’s regional groups to ensure geographical representation. And for the second year in a row, all regional groups put forward the exact number of candidates for available seats for the three-year term, resulting in uncontested races.

“This uncompetitive vote makes a mockery of the word ‘election’,” said Louis Charbonneau, UN director at Human Rights Watch.

“No one should have a seat on this crucial body handed to them on a silver platter”, Charbonneau said.

He called on UN member nations to “insist on competitive slates so they can reject candidates with poor human rights records”.

In Tuesday’s vote, the Africa group’s Zambia, Ghana, Nigeria and Burundi were elected.

The Asia-Pacific group’s Kuwait, Nepal, Jordan and Japan won seats, as did Brazil, the Dominican Republic and Uruguay from the Latin America and Caribbean group.

Ireland and Germany from the mainly Western group, and Moldova and Ukraine from the Central and East European group, will also join the Human Rights Council.

The Geneva-based council reviews the human rights records of all countries periodically, appoints independent investigators to report on issues such as torture and situations in countries such as North Korea, Iran and Myanmar, and sends fact-finding missions to investigate rights violations. These include missions in Ukraine, the occupied Palestinian territories and Israel, and Sudan.

The council was created in 2006 to replace a human rights commission discredited because some members had poor rights records. But the new council soon faced similar criticism, including that countries sought seats to protect themselves and their allies.

Soon after starting his second term, US President Donald Trump announced the withdrawal of Washington from the Human Rights Council, accusing it of anti-Israel bias. He also pulled the US out in his first term.

UN spokesman Stephane Dujarric, responding to a question about the UN position on the uncontested vote, said it was a matter for the 193 member nations.

“But what we’ve always said is that member states who are elected to this organisation’s highest human rights body have an added responsibility to protect human rights,” he said.

images.caption: The UN logo is seen during the 81st United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York on September 26, 2026 [Charly Triballeau/AFP]

articles.title: U.S. halts prosecution of former CIA analyst accused of aiding South Korean intelligence
articles.summary: Federal prosecutors said Sue Mi Terry shared nonpublic government information and accepted luxury gifts in exchange for advocating South Korean government positions.
articles.body: The Justice Department has agreed not to prosecute a former CIA analyst who in 2024 was accused of serving as a secret agent for South Korea’s intelligence service, according to court documents filed Tuesday. Federal prosecutors said Sue Mi Terry shared nonpublic government information, facilitated access for South Korean officials to U.S. officials and accepted luxury gifts in exchange for advocating South Korean government positions during media appearances. The Justice Department agreed Tuesday to put her prosecution on hold for a year and then drop the charges altogether if Terry stays out of legal trouble. The deal comes weeks before Terry was set to stand trial in a Manhattan federal court on charges of acting as an unregistered foreign agent. Prosecutors did not explain in court documents why they decided not to move forward with her case, saying only that they determined that the interests of both Terry and the U.S. “will be best served by deferring prosecution.” The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Terry had maintained her innocence. Her attorney, Lee Wolosky, said Tuesday that Terry had “served her country loyally for many years” and was pleased with this result. “We have consistently maintained that her interactions with South Korean officials were conducted in furtherance of U.S. interests and her work as a leading American specialist on North Korea and East Asia,” Wolosky said in a statement. As part of her deal, Terry signed a document agreeing to certain facts of the case, including that she had shared notes with a South Korean intelligence officer from an off-the-record meeting she attended with then-U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken in 2022. The document also said she accepted designer handbags and coats from South Korea’s intelligence service for her work, which were collectively valued at about $9,245.

images.caption: Sue Mi Terry attends the 50th Telluride Film Festival on September 02, 2023 in Telluride, Colorado.

articles.title: UN official says ‘window of opportunity’ for peace in DR Congo
articles.summary: The envoy lauds the progress in diplomatic efforts despite the worsening security and humanitarian situation.
articles.body:
A senior United Nations official has told the Security Council there is a “window of opportunity” for peace in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, a mineral-rich region plagued by decades of conflict.

Huang Xia, the UN special envoy for the impacted Great Lakes Region, on Tuesday said that both US- and Qatar-led peace processes have achieved “notable progress”.

However, “despite this sustained diplomatic effort, the security and humanitarian situation in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo has continued to worsen”, he added.

Several parties, including the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group and the Congolese army, have clashed in the territory, prompting a series of international diplomatic efforts.

Huang stressed the “urgency of seizing the window of opportunity, which is currently offered by the increased alignment of peace efforts”.

“Such a window does not remain open indefinitely,” he said.

“I therefore urge all parties to translate commitments into verifiable actions, and to place their trust in confidence built through deeds rather than through declarations.”

The Congolese government and the M23 signed a commitment towards a ceasefire in Doha in July 2025. The DRC and Rwanda also formalised a US-brokered peace deal in December in Washington, DC.

However, fighting has continued on the ground.

New talks were held in August in Switzerland, involving representatives from the United States, Qatar and the African Union.

Huang said the UN would facilitate a meeting on October 18 in Zambia’s capital, Lusaka, between the defence ministers of Burundi, the DRC, Uganda, Rwanda and Tanzania.

images.caption: Armed security personnel keep watch during a collective memorial service organised by the Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC) and the M23 armed group in Masisi, North Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo, on January 8, 2026 [Moise Kasereka/EPA]

articles.title: How did five baby orangutans end up abandoned in India?
articles.summary: CNN has spent weeks investigating the shadowy, brutal trade in which endangered animals are poached and moved through networks of brokers across borders and seas.
articles.body: Huddled and frightened, adjusting to an alien environment, five newly orphaned babies lay inexplicably in the forest’s undergrowth. With shaggy, reddish-orange fur, wide eyes and long limbs, they were unlike any other animal found in this corner of eastern India. They were soon surrounded by a crowd of about 1,000 bewildered villagers, who alerted forest officials patrolling nearby. When officers arrived, they were stunned. The animals were baby orangutans: critically endangered great apes; some of the world’s most intelligent animals, and a species prized by private collectors. They belong thousands of kilometers away, in the Southeast Asian rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra. Yet here they were in India’s Odisha state, all under 18 months old, separated from their mothers, and then abandoned. Pratik Prakash Indalkar, a forest officer from Balasore, a coastal city in eastern Odisha, told CNN his staff were not sure how to handle the find, which he characterized as “very surprising.” Their discovery gripped India. For days, the plight of the Odisha quintet dominated headlines and primetime broadcasts. Yet for conservationists, their ordeal is a grim reminder of a far larger reality: a $20 billion illicit trade that tears critically endangered animals from their habitats and traffics them with ruthless efficiency. Indonesia’s government says the available evidence suggests the babies originated in Sumatra, the massive island in the west of the archipelago nation. Since their discovery, CNN has spent weeks investigating the shadowy, brutal trade in which endangered animals are poached and moved through networks of brokers across borders and seas. Drawing on conversations with wildlife sellers, social media posts and interviews with nearly a dozen experts, including environmentalists, researchers and a former trafficker, we chart the likely journey that took these orangutans from Indonesia to India. It is a journey that almost certainly began with violence. To capture an infant orangutan, poachers typically must first kill its mother, who will fiercely defend her young. By the time these babies reached India, they had likely endured weeks of fear, hunger and dehydration. They showed little interest in climbing nearby trees – unusual behavior for these arboreal animals, who spend their lives in the forest canopy and rarely descend to the ground. Authorities rushed in food and water before transporting the babies to a nearby government office. Video from the rescue shows them being carefully carried away before making the nearly 400-kilometer (250-mile) trip to Nandankanan Zoo. There, they remain in quarantine, far from the forests where they were born and the mothers they lost. And their story is just one of many in the illegal wildlife trafficking industry. Deep in the humid greenery of a Sumatran rainforest, serenaded by birdsong and the jungle’s endless thrum, a baby orangutan clings to its mother. Their bond, like all maternal bonds in primates, is incredibly difficult to break. Orangutans are among nature’s most devoted mothers, rarely letting babies out of reach, and raising their young for up to nine years. Young orangutans learn the essentials of survival from their mothers: how to forage, swing through the canopy and avoid danger. Several experts say this is why poachers in the illegal wildlife trade often kill the mother first. “To me, it’s almost certain they were taken from the wild,” said Lionel Hachemin, global director of the Wildlife Crime Program at the International Fund for Animal Welfare. “Obtaining five orangutan infants of the same age would be extraordinarily difficult, even for the world’s best-resourced breeding facilities. It would require years of coordinated effort, an ideal breeding population, and at least 20 adult females.” Conservationists who have spent decades tracking the trade describe the process as ruthless and predictable. “If you find one baby orangutan, it means one mother orangutan has died,” said Binur D. Naibaho, director of Sustainable Landscape at the Orangutan Information Centre (OIC), a non-governmental organization based in North Sumatra. Naibaho described how some villagers in Sumatra are paid up to 15 million Indonesian rupiah ($846) to poach a baby orangutan. “The local people will hunt the orangutan, kill the mother and take the baby and give to the agent to go to the black market,” he said. The mother’s protective instinct becomes her death sentence. “There is no way that the mother would leave her baby,” according to Femke den Haas, co-founder and director of Jakarta Animal Aid Network (JAAN) Indonesia. “She will fight for her baby till the end.” Once the mother is dead, poachers wrench the infant from her chest. “The baby will still be clinging onto the mother, holding on really tight, screaming.” In moments, the baby becomes an orphan and loses everything it knows: the rhythm of its mother’s heartbeat, her protection, and the only bond it has in the world. Then comes a terrifying journey into captivity. It could have taken anywhere from one to three weeks to convey the babies from source to India, according to Hachemin. “Our experience is that syndicates try to minimize transit time for live animals such as great apes because the mortality rate makes delays expensive, thus impacting profits,” he said. The conditions they were transported in may never be known. But testimony, videos and photographs shared with CNN by conservationists offer a window into the suffering these animals often endure during trafficking. “You’re being placed in a dark box, moved to different locations,” den Haas said, adding that many don’t make it because of the harsh conditions. Posing as a potential buyer several years ago, conservation photojournalist Paul Hilton recalled being led deep into a rural Sumatran community after a tip-off of an orangutan for sale. The animal’s treatment laid bare the cruelty of the illegal wildlife trade. “Every time it started to move, they slapped it on the head,” Hilton said. “It’s suffering and getting a little bit of rice every day. Maybe a bit of fruit now and again.” The orangutan was rescued and now lives in a rehabilitation center. Other footage shared with CNN by JAAN Indonesia shows similarly grim scenes. In one video, a young orangutan can be seen crouching in the corner of a small, dark crate, its frightened eyes wide open. Den Haas said the infant was one of two hidden beneath bananas and luggage on a passenger bus in southern Sumatra. They were discovered by JAAN’s wildlife detection dog. “They were extremely scared, they were less than a year (old), and they were in a very bad condition,” den Haas said. “The trauma of that can last for years. Some never truly recover.” Providing a faint ray of hope in this otherwise bleak start to life, the five baby orangutans have been settling into their new surroundings in Odisha at the Nandankanan Zoo. Veterinarians are closely monitoring their health, tracking their temperature, and providing daily updates on their condition. For comfort, the orphans have been given orangutan plush toys. They haven’t been given names yet, but the babies have started recognizing their carers. The slightly older babies are “climbing and swinging,” said the zoo’s deputy director, Pradeep Mirase. The younger ones keep clinging to each other. Rescuers who transported the animals to the zoo moved at a painstaking pace, carefully navigating every bump and turn to avoid stressing or injuring them, said Indalkar from the forest department in Odisha. “We had to give them cushioning and something to play with, because they would get stressed without it. We had staff inside the vehicle, and insulated ice boxes on hand, since we weren’t sure about ventilation,” he said. “We also had (straw) for them, to make them feel more at home.” Orangutans are classified as “critically endangered” on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. An estimated 104,000 Bornean orangutans, 13,000 Sumatran orangutans, and just 800 Tapanuli orangutans remain in the wild, according to the World Wildlife Fund. Decades of deforestation have devastated vast areas of orangutan habitat, pushing the animals into smaller pockets, increasing their vulnerability to poachers. Currently, raging wildfires in West Kalimantan, Borneo, further threaten their survival. International trade of Sumatran orangutans is prohibited under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), and the species is protected under Indonesian law. Yet, trafficking these apes is a criminal enterprise that spans multiple countries, fueled by a lucrative black-market demand for exotic pets, experts say; demand from people who admire the animals enough to covet one, but are paradoxically callous to the suffering their purchase inflicts. CNN spoke to a former wildlife trafficker, who described the trade as a sophisticated machine; a syndicate that involves poachers, brokers, sellers and smugglers. He said he spent years collecting exotic animals as a hobby before realizing around 2012 that he could make money from the trade. His business started with baby gibbons and other primates, Komodo dragons, exotic birds and wild cats – animals he would usually buy directly from poachers. He agreed to speak with CNN on condition of anonymity, to avoid retribution for speaking out. We’re calling him Budi. Budi said profit was his primary motivation. “It’s easy money,” he said. “You give me the money, I give you the animals. Then that’s it. The deal is over.” Budi said he was once offered an orangutan from a poacher for 30 million rupiah ($1,668), which he could then go on to sell for about 10 times that on the international market. He ultimately turned it down, because it is “really hard work to keep them alive.” He explained that wildlife trafficking relies on a network of actors, each playing a distinct role. After poachers or hunters capture an animal, they sell it to intermediaries like Budi, who then resell it at a profit. The supply chain also includes transporters or couriers responsible for moving the animals, and specialist marketers who connect sellers with potential buyers. In recent years, some poachers and traders have increasingly turned to middlemen to broker transactions and facilitate sales. “Every seller has their own hunters or poachers, and every seller has their own specialized marketers,” Budi said. “Every seller tries to hide their identity. Mostly they do not have a link with another seller. They just interact by the middleman if they have a transaction.” Budi said he gave little thought to the animals’ ordeal, or to the suffering they endured after being poached from the wild and trafficked. “Sometimes some of the animals died, some of them got sick,” he said. “We just get rid of the sick and the diseased ones.” Budi did most of his selling on social media platforms and said he’d be concerned about being caught after every transaction. “You’re doing the illegal activity, so every time you are getting concerned.” But ultimately, he said, wildlife trafficking is not a dangerous industry to be a part of, citing poor law enforcement and punishment. In 2024, Indonesia revised its anti-wildlife trafficking law to bring in stricter fines and longer jail sentences. Individuals can now be fined as much as $5 billion rupiah ($280,000) and jailed up to 15 years. But Budi said many traffickers spend about a year and a half in prison and return to the illegal trade after their release. CNN has contacted Indonesia’s Ministry of Forestry and its national police force for a response. Budi stopped trafficking animals in 2019, after a friend warned him that he could go to jail, and he now works as an informant on wildlife crime for a non-governmental organization. “It’s like you just paid the sin, and it’s really good just working for the future of the animals and the nature itself.” Based on known trafficking routes, experts say the baby orangutans’ journey to India likely started in Indonesia’s Aceh province, at Sumatra’s northern tip. From there, they likely boarded small fishing vessels for the journey to Thailand, one of the region’s most important wildlife trafficking hubs, according to multiple conservationists and researchers familiar with the route. Investigators and conservation groups say this is often the stage where animals are moved between trafficking networks before continuing toward their final destination. If that destination is India, the trail then likely moves overland into Myanmar, a segment of the route that is significantly murkier, according to Hachemin. Wildlife is believed to travel through a series of border crossings linking Thailand and Myanmar, including the Mae Sot-Myawaddy and Tachileik-Mae Sai corridors, both of which have long been associated with all manner of illicit trafficking. However, five years of civil war in Myanmar has altered trafficking patterns. With some roads blocked or heavily controlled, traffickers are increasingly believed to be using secondary roads and remote jungle trails, making movements harder to track. The final leg of the journey takes the animals across the India-Myanmar border. Experts from the Wildlife Trust of India (WTI) identified two principal Indian entry points: the northeastern states of Manipur and Mizoram. Open-source data gathered by the WTI and shared with CNN showed 23 cases of illegal wildlife trafficking-related seizures in India’s northeast states between 2015 and 2026. The most frequently seized commodities, it said, were pangolin scales and live pangolins, followed by live exotic non-native mammals, including primates. The data indicates there may be more such cases. “My suspicion is that (the five orangutans) must have come through the northeastern land border which is porous and which is also the preferred border,” said Jose Louies, WTI’s chief executive. “You have to look at the low-risk border. So, if I am a smuggler, I will be using the northeastern border to bring the animals in.” They could have also traveled via Bangladesh, according to several experts. Dwi Adhiasto, an Indonesian wildlife conservationist and criminologist, said he has been detecting the smuggling of wildlife, including primates, into Mizoram since around 2015. The state is a “key transit point,” said Adhiasto, senior technical adviser with the Science for Endangered and Trafficked Species (SCENTS) Foundation, an Indonesian non-profit that works to combat endangered wildlife trafficking and poaching. He added it “serves as a heavy end point or transit point for wildlife from Indonesia.” While the industry’s trafficking routes are kept obscured, its advertising is done in the open. Primates of all kinds – including endangered species like slow lorises and gibbons – are advertised blatantly in public Facebook groups. Photos and videos show them caged, leashed or clothed, or cuddling children to highlight their gentle temperament. CNN spoke to several sellers advertising animals online in lengthy conversations over several days, who claimed they could ship them internationally using regular regional air couriers like J&T Express. “There won’t be any issues with customs,” one Indonesia-based suspected trafficker told CNN when asked about shipping a monkey to Mumbai. “If you place your order now, you can receive the baby monkey and pick it up at the airport within seven hour (sic),” he says, explaining that a flight attendant will hand over the animal. The traffickers appear to know the animals well, commenting on their preferences and personalities. “It’s a bit fierce… like a tiger cub,” another trafficker says about a jungle cat. The animals are said to be caught from the wild. In videos sent by the traffickers, a group of small monkeys stare wide-eyed at the camera as they cling to one another. Others huddle in the corner of a cage. Asked whether the animals will need any certificates to fly across the continent, one user advertising wildlife simply responds that the animal is “illegal.” Facebook owner Meta’s website says it prohibits content that “attempts to buy, sell, trade, donate or gift or asks for endangered species or their parts.” The company told CNN it will get the Facebook groups investigated. CNN has reached out to J&T for comment. Its website says it prohibits the delivery of dead or living animals. We may never know the exact route the five orangutans took on their multinational odyssey, but some clues have emerged about what happened once they reached India. CCTV footage from Digha, a coastal town in West Bengal bordering Odisha, captured what’s believed to be a handoff involving two vehicles, including a black SUV and a white car, according to Indian media reports citing investigators. Authorities are examining whether one of those vehicles transported the animals before they were ultimately abandoned in Odisha’s forests, the reports said. Authorities are also looking into a Digha hotel and its owners to determine whether the animals were kept there. Three individuals were temporarily detained, according to local reports. Multiple officials contacted by CNN declined to comment on the ongoing investigation. According to IFAW’s Hachemin, these are the hallmarks of a multi-layered trafficking network designed to obscure the identities of key players. “This pattern suggests sanitized handoffs,” said Hachemin, adding that the objective is to create distance between suppliers, transporters, and eventual buyers. This all raises the question of why the orangutans were abandoned, alone on the forest ground. Did traffickers hastily ditch their extremely valuable cargo, maybe after being spooked by nearby patrols? Were the animals dropped with the intention that some other criminal operatives would come and pick them up for the next leg of their journey? Or were they, for some reason, intended to be found by the authorities? Some experts told CNN they believe India was likely meant to serve as the destination, rather than a transit hub. Based on previous patterns, they said, the babies were likely intended to become part of someone’s private pet collection or placed in an unlicensed zoo. Fahmi Prayoga, minister counsellor at Indonesia’s embassy in New Delhi, said a delegation from Indonesia is expected to visit India to carry out a DNA and morphology test on the animals. He said authorities in both countries are cooperating to ensure the infants are sent to their rightful home, and urged the two to work together to combat illegal wildlife trafficking. “We have to do this together,” he said. CNN has contacted India’s Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, and the foreign ministry, for a response. For now, the five young orangutans are safe, and may yet live happier, healthier lives than they faced at their intended destination. For the people now caring for them, the road ahead will be long. The traumatized orphans must slowly be taught the survival skills they should be learning from their mothers. For Indalkar, the forest officer from Balasore, protecting the orangutans is a responsibility that weighs heavily on every handler. “This is a very big asset,” he said. “Five babies like this, it’s like an international treasure.”

articles.title: A trial over one of the biggest acts of sabotage in decades is getting underway. Here’s a refresher
articles.summary: A Ukrainian national goes on trial in Germany accused of involvement in the Nord Stream pipeline attack, one of the biggest acts of sabotage in modern history
articles.body: It started with a stream of bubbles rising to the surface of the Baltic Sea. Seven months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, explosions burst through two Nord Stream gas pipelines – Russia’s controversial gas highway into Europe – in the waters between Sweden and Poland. Investigators from several countries raced to determine who was responsible and fingers were immediately pointed at Russia. Then, two Ukrainian nationals were arrested, raising questions about state involvement and presenting a test of loyalty for some of Kyiv’s European allies. On Wednesday, one of them will go on trial in Germany accused of involvement in one of the biggest – and most mysterious – acts of sabotage in modern history. He denies wrongdoing and Ukraine has denied any involvement. Here’s what you need to know: What is Nord Stream and what happened? Nord Stream 1 and 2 are two major conduits created to funnel Russian gas to Europe, via Germany. Owned by Nord Stream AG, whose majority shareholder is the Russian gas firm Gazprom, the pipelines were divisive even before the start of the Ukraine war, mainly due to concerns over European reliance on cheap Russian hydrocarbons. Nord Stream 1 was announced in 1997, when relations between the West and post-Soviet Russia were relatively calm, and became operational in 2011. Nord Stream 2, a sister project, was completed in September 2021, but never entered service. Germany shelved it days before Moscow invaded Ukraine. In late September 2022, explosions ripped through the two pipelines near the Danish island of Bornholm, releasing plumes of gas into the surrounding water and sparking a cross-border investigation. How did the investigation unfold? Sweden was the first country to sound the alarm on the leaks. Some experts at the time said they could have been caused by a technical malfunction, but the leaders of several Western countries were quick to identify sabotage as the likely cause. Two months after the event, Swedish prosecutors announced the incident was a result of “gross sabotage,” adding that “traces of explosives” had been found at the scene. Although neither pipeline was in operation at the time of the attack, both still contained gas under pressure. As a result, experts said an “unprecedented” amount of the greenhouse gases might have leaked into the atmosphere. Several agencies were tasked with digging into the attack, including German, Danish and Scandinavian security authorities. European officials vowed a firm response. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said any deliberate act to disrupt Europe’s energy infrastructure was “unacceptable” and would “lead to the strongest response possible.” Germany in particular was keen to see the alleged culprits brought to justice and, in 2024, authorities there issued an international arrest warrant for a Ukrainian man suspected of involvement. Since then, two Ukrainian men have been arrested over their alleged role in the pipeline attacks. Denmark and Sweden both closed their criminal investigations into the explosions in 2024, with Sweden citing a lack of jurisdiction and Denmark saying there were not sufficient grounds to pursue the case. This left Berlin the only nation to pursue the leads. Who is on trial? Serhii Kuznietsov, a former Ukrainian soldier, is the lone defendant in the trial starting Wednesday in Hamburg, where he is identified only as Serhii K under German privacy laws. German prosecutors said he “belongs to a group of people who planted explosive devices in the gas pipelines Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 near the island of Bornholm in September 2022.” Prosecutors have accused Serhii K of being an accomplice to the “war crime” of attacking civilian objects, destruction of infrastructure, causing an explosion and disrupting public operations, according to court filings. The court filings accused him of “acting on behalf of Ukrainian state authorities” in an alleged plot to destroy the Nord Stream pipelines. His defense lawyer previously told CNN that he denies any wrongdoing. In 2025, Kuznietsov was arrested by Italian police in Rimini – a city in northern Italy known for its sandy beaches and Roman landmarks – and later extradited to Germany. Prosecutors in Germany believe he and his accomplices used a sailing yacht to carry out the attack, traveling from the port of Rostock, a city in northern Germany. The vessel had been rented from a German company via intermediaries using forged identity documents, prosecutors claim. The second Ukrainian man arrested in connection with the bombing, Volodymyr Zhuravlov, was detained in August in Croatia, where a court has approved his extradition to Germany, Reuters reported last month. His lawyer dismissed the ruling and said he could appeal the decision, Reuters added. German prosecutors said he was “strongly suspected” of several criminal offenses, including sabotage and causing an explosion, and participating in dives to the pipelines. Zhuravlov was previously arrested in Poland, which declined to extradite him to Germany. How does this link to the wider war? The explosions rang out at a tense time for Europe. The attacks heightened the controversy over Europe’s use of Russian gas and put Germany – the driving force behind the gas project – under the spotlight over former chancellor Angela Merkel’s decision to adopt a conciliatory approach to Moscow despite its recent aggression toward Ukraine and Georgia. Donald Tusk, the prime minister of Ukraine’s close ally Poland, said last year that Europe’s problem was “not that Nord Stream 2 was blown up, but that it was built.” As far back as 2007, Poland’s then-defense minister Radek Sikorski railed against the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, then under construction, calling it “the most outrageous attempt by Mr Putin to divide and damage the EU.” When Zhuravlov was initially arrested in Poland, a judge ruled against his extradition to Germany, saying that if the Nord Stream blasts were an act of Ukrainian sabotage, it would be a justified response to an unprovoked invasion. With court officials saying Wednesday’s trial is expected to run until February next year, Germany will be hoping no new roadblocks lie ahead as it seeks to get to the truth of this murky affair.

articles.title: Jamaica begins receiving third-country deportees under controversial U.S. agreement
articles.summary: The first flight transporting third-country nationals from the United States arrived in Jamaica on Tuesday, marking the commencement of a highly scrutinized bilateral agreement that utilizes the Caribbean nation as a temporary transit hub for migrants.
articles.body: KINGSTON, Jamaica — The first flight transporting third-country nationals from the United States arrived in Jamaica on Tuesday, marking the commencement of a highly scrutinized bilateral agreement that utilizes the Caribbean nation as a temporary transit hub for migrants. These agreements, whose legality will be debated by the Supreme Court, have become increasingly common under the Trump administration, with migrants being sent to Liberia, Eswatini, Paraguay and beyond. The group of 22 migrants — all adults including seven women — were quickly processed on arrival at Kingston’s Norman Manley International Airport mid-afternoon Tuesday and whisked away by bus with police escort to an undisclosed location. The media was not given access. Jamaican authorities say they are following procedures intended to ensure the arrangement’s implementation in a “safe, orderly and lawful manner.” The flight’s arrival marks the operational beginning of a bilateral memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in June this year. Under the arrangement, non-Jamaican migrants will be flown to the Caribbean nation before being transferred to their home countries or other destinations. While official passenger manifests and exact arrival times were closely guarded, local sources indicated the inaugural cohort consisted largely of South American nationals. The Jamaican government has previously confirmed that the program will strictly cap arrivals, accepting “a maximum of 25 persons per fortnight.” Both the Ministry of National Security and Peace and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade again sought to reassure the public about the deal’s parameters on Tuesday. “The government reiterates that this is a transit arrangement intended to facilitate the return of Third Country Nationals to their country of origin or other receiving countries, with the support of the IOM (International Organization for Migration),” the joint statement read. “The arrangement will not be funded by the Government of Jamaica,” the release stated, adding that “no third-country national with criminal antecedents will be permitted to transit through Jamaica.” The ministries emphasized their commitment to transparency and international standards. The framework of the agreement relies heavily on the International Organization for Migration (IOM), which will manage housing and logistics through its Assisted Voluntary Return program. Public anxiety over these logistics has simmered for months. In June, the Ministry of National Security publicly dismissed “false and misleading” claims that migrants would be housed in the rural parish of St. Mary, clarifying that any housing arrangements were strictly the IOM’s responsibility. Despite these assurances, the rollout has sparked intense political friction in Kingston. The agreement has been sharply criticized by local politicians and transparency advocates who argue that the Jamaican Parliament was entirely bypassed during negotiations and that undisclosed details remain hidden. “Jamaicans are being asked to trust a secret document that touches their security, their communities and their public services,” argued Fitz Jackson, the opposition spokesperson on national security. Jackson previously said that failing to table the executed MOU in Parliament is a “blatant contempt to the people of Jamaica.” Mark Golding, Jamaica’s Opposition Leader, has repeatedly challenged the administration to explain what tangible benefits the country extracts from the arrangement. Responding to sustained criticisms, Foreign Affairs Minister Kamina Johnson Smith said Tuesday on X: “We have made every effort to negotiate this transit agreement with protection of Jamaica and the Jamaican people in mind.” She added there is nothing “prejudicial” in the agreement, but the U.S. has not agreed to make it public. The unease extends beyond the political sphere. Bishop Alvin Bailey, leader of a local evangelical alliance, has expressed deep skepticism, asking why the U.S. could not deport the individuals directly to their home countries. “We just don’t trust what the government is saying,” Bailey said previously.

articles.title: CJP's Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka: India's 'cockroach' leaders jailed after holding protest
articles.summary: The youth leaders were sent to custody on charges of trespassing at Jantar Mantar, a now denotified protest site.
articles.body:
Two top leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) have been sent to jail for five days after being arrested for allegedly trespassing at a protest site in Delhi.

Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka appeared before a magistrate on Wednesday after being detained at Jantar Mantar, a longstanding venue for demonstrations that police recently removed from the city's list of authorised protest sites.

The two were among a group who climbed a locked gate and crossed barricades to enter the site on Tuesday.

The GenZ-led movement has been protesting for days seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of India's top election official over allegations of vote fraud - charges the poll panel denies.

Police accused Das, Ranka and their fellow activist Ajinkya Shinde of trespassing, breaching a peace bond, violating prohibitory orders and obstructing public officials - charges they deny.

Delhi's Special Executive Magistrate Court remanded Das and Ranka to five days in judicial custody, while Shinde was released on a personal bond. The two leaders can seek bail from a higher court.

Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, who has been holding separate protests against the Election Commission, condemned the arrests, describing them as "an act of cowardice", and expressed support for peaceful demonstrations at Jantar Mantar.

"Students. Youth. Journalists. The [opposition's] INDIA bloc. Different banners, one cause. All protests are one: citizens demanding their constitutional rights," he wrote on X.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, who was travelling to Delhi after the arrests, accused the government of cracking down on dissent and challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi to "declare the Emergency officially", according to news agency PTI.

His comments drew parallels with India's 1970s Emergency, a period when civil liberties were curtailed under then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.

The CJP, which is a pressure group and not an official political party, has been demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.

Wednesday's actions follow a weekend of protests during which Das, Ranka, Shinde, and Dipke were taken into preventive custody ahead of planned demonstrations at Jantar Mantar. They were later released by a magistrate.

Police imposed extensive security restrictions across Delhi, closing several metro stations and deploying thousands of police and paramilitary personnel to prevent demonstrators from reaching the site. Thousands of people, including journalists, were detained and later released, while videos showed police forcibly dragging some protesters into buses.

Following the weekend protests, Delhi police removed Jantar Mantar from its list of authorised protest sites, instead designating three other venues - Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground.

The CJP criticised the decision, saying it would make demonstrations less visible and harder for protesters to make their voices heard.

On Tuesday, the activists returned to Jantar Mantar despite the restrictions. Videos shared by Dipke and other CJP leaders showed Das and Ranka climbing over police barricades, carrying Indian flags and chanting slogans.

"You cannot denotify the resistance," Dipke wrote on X.

Ratna Singh, head of the CJP's legal team, alleged that the activists were denied access to lawyers for several hours before being taken to Parliament Street Police Station in a private vehicle at about 03:00 local time (21:30 GMT on Tuesday).

She also rejected a police allegation that CJP leaders had called on others to join the protest at Jantar Mantar.

"Absolutely false! No public call was ever made," she wrote on X.

The CJP emerged from student-led demonstrations earlier this year over alleged exam irregularities and demands for education reforms.

Weeks of protests led by the movement culminated in the resignation of federal Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

The group began as an online satire movement after India's Chief Justice Surya Kant compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches during a court hearing in May.

He later said his remarks had been misinterpreted, but the comments had already become a rallying cry for young people demanding change.

Following the summer protests, the CJP developed into a wider pressure group, tapping into discontent over unemployment, examinations and government accountability.

The CJP launched its latest nationwide protests in Mumbai on 2 October, following an Indian Express report alleging that Chief Election Commissioner Kumar had ignored objections from his two fellow commissioners over changes to voter registration.

The newspaper reported that commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised concerns at least 14 times over 10 months about decisions taken without their knowledge, including changes affecting voter databases and electoral rolls. The Election Commission has denied the allegations, saying its decisions were unanimous.

The controversy has intensified scrutiny of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, a voter verification exercise that opposition parties allege has benefited Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The Election Commission and the government denies this.

Although the CJP and opposition parties have not held joint protests, their demonstrations have coincided in recent days. Gandhi is among politicians, lawyers and journalists detained during protests across several cities.

articles.title: China and North Korea to open New Yalu River Bridge, state media reports
articles.summary: The long-delayed bridge will formally open on Thursday, according to China’s state-run Xinhua news agency.
articles.body:
China and North Korea will officially open the New Yalu River Bridge to traffic on Thursday, China’s state-run Xinhua news agency reports.

China completed its side of the bridge in 2014, hoping to boost trade ties. However, North Korea left its side unfinished for years as relations soured after Beijing supported United Nations sanctions over Pyongyang’s nuclear tests.

The first bridge connecting Russia and North Korea also opened earlier this month.

China’s exports to North Korea rose to a six-year high of $2.3bn last year, a 25 percent increase from the previous year. Chinese President Xi Jinping was welcomed in Pyongyang in June for the first time since 2019.

Since 2018, Beijing has tried to repair ties with Pyongyang, which also briefly began improving relations with Washington around the same time.

The China-North Korea relationship was forged during the Korean War. In 1961, the two countries signed the Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance, which remains China’s only formal military alliance.

The treaty contains a mutual defence clause committing either side to assist the other if one comes under armed attack.

Although China was North Korea’s main diplomatic partner and protector for decades, relations strained after Beijing in 2017 supported tightening sanctions on Pyongyang for its nuclear weapons programme.

Analysts say North Korea’s recent growing relationship with Russia may have changed the balance of Pyongyang’s diplomatic dependence, reducing its reliance on Beijing.

North Korea and Russia signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty in 2024, including a mutual defence provision. Military and political ties between the two countries have grown considerably stronger, with North Korea deploying thousands of troops to fight in Russia’s war on Ukraine.

United States President Donald Trump also signalled an interest in repairing relations with Pyongyang last month, after his talks with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un abruptly ended in 2019. In his second term, Trump has floated meeting Kim again, though no official meeting has been set.

North Korea has not yet resumed issuing tourism visas to Chinese citizens, who once made up the bulk of its overseas visitors.

While North Korea’s trade with Russia largely involves military supplies, exchanges with China could arguably involve goods North Korea needs to develop its civilian economy, analysts have said.

articles.title: Life as a offshore wind turbine worker in the North Sea
articles.summary: The BBC joins technicians on a voyage to the Westermost Rough wind farm off the Yorkshire coast.
articles.body:
Wind farms are a familiar sight off the coast of Britain, but what goes into maintaining them? At Westermost Rough, in the North Sea, a team of workers are tasked with ensuring 35 gigantic turbines keep generating electricity.

That involves climbing the turbine towers almost 300ft (90m) high above the water, as the BBC discovered when we joined workers on a voyage to the site about five miles from Withernsea, East Yorkshire.

When we set out on a crew transfer vessel from Grimsby docks on a bright October morning, the sea is unusually calm.

"It's like a sheet of glass," says our pilot Peter Gracey as he looks out across the calm sea.

Westermost Rough is operated by Orsted and can generate enough electricity to power more than 180,000 homes.

As we approach heading north from Spurn Point, at the tip of the Yorkshire coast, the turbines are standing still.

The lack of wind means the blades are idle, but for maintenance crews it is close to perfect working weather.

In the distance, another bright yellow crew transfer vessel can be seen moving between turbines, ferrying engineers from one maintenance job to the next.

Days like this are prized by crews. Calm seas make it easier to transfer workers safely from vessel to turbine and mean engineers can carry out inspections and repairs that might otherwise have to wait.

Sam Torrance is among the technicians who carries out these tasks.

A former apprentice from Healing, near Grimsby, he has worked for Orsted for the past seven years.

For Torrance, the job is equal parts detective work and engineering.

"I'm a troubleshooter," he says. "The office will tell me something's broken and I have to go and find out why it's broken and I'll go and fix it."

The work often starts long before he reaches the turbine itself. Modern offshore wind farms send a stream of data back to shore, reporting everything from power output and wind speeds to pressure readings and fault codes.

"We get a lot of feedback," he explains. "The turbine will send fault codes, it'll send pressures, it'll send what the wind speeds are and how much electricity it's producing."

Staff back at base use the data to prepare Torrance for the maintenance work.

"They might pick me 20 parts or 100 parts. I might end up only needing one of them."

During the summer months, crews race to complete servicing programmes before rougher weather arrives.

"You don't want to fall behind over the winter," he adds.

As our Windcat vessel approaches one of the turbines, Gracey manoeuvres it into place.

Able Seaman David Higgins then oversees the transfer of technicians from boat to turbine – a process governed by strict safety procedures.

"It's almost like a taxi service, which is why it's called a crew transfer vessel," Higgins says.

The engines push the vessel firmly against the turbine's access ladder, holding it securely in place. Torrance and his colleagues then attach themselves to a fall-arrest system before beginning the ascent to a work platform.

On a calm day, the transfer looks straightforward. In rougher weather it can be anything but.

"If there's any big waves you would stop everything until it's clear," Higgins explains.

Once aboard the platform, crew members face a trip to the top of the turbine tower, helped sometimes, but not always, by a built-in lift.

For Torrance, having to climb up can be one of the most physically demanding parts of the job.

"It's exhausting," he says. "Your lungs burn. The air is thick. If the lift is out of use, it's a bad day."

Tools and equipment are lifted up to the turbine by crane before technicians begin diagnosing faults, replacing components or carrying out planned servicing.

Despite the pressure to return turbines to service, Torrance says there is no pressure to cut corners.

"The job takes as long as it takes," he adds.

Westermost Rough is approaching the midpoint of its estimated operational life. It was designed to operate for 25 years and was the first in the world to make commercial use of Siemens 6MW offshore wind turbines, with components built in Hull .

Three other wind farms, Hornsea 1, 2 and 3, have been constructed nearby, but in 2025, Orsted decided to "discontinue" Hornsea 4 , which would have been one of the country's largest, saying it no longer made economic sense.

In August this year, the company said it was " evaluating options for future development " at the site.

In January, the government awarded contracts to build a record amount of offshore wind around the UK, arguing that these projects are cheaper than new gas power stations and will "bring down bills for good".

However, at the time, the Conservatives said climate targets and increasing costs in the sector were raising energy prices.

The way engineers work could also change in the years ahead.

Last week, Orsted announced successful trials of large cargo drones , capable of delivering tools and spare parts directly to offshore turbines, potentially reducing lifting operations and helping maintenance teams respond more quickly.

For now, however, offshore wind still very much depends on people like Torrance.

As the vessel returns to Grimsby at the end of the day, he reflects on an industry that has shaped his own career and, to some extent, the Humber's economy.

"It's rewarding at the end of the day," he says. "Amazing to be a part of."

articles.title: Hotel to be built on former Wakefield Westgate station site
articles.summary: The hotel on what was Wakefield Westgate rail station will "meet growing demand", the council says.
articles.body:
Work on a new city centre hotel at the site of a former railway station will begin in 2027, it has been confirmed.

The hotel will be built on the site of the former Wakefield Westgate station and when completed it would "meet growing demand" from visitors and business travellers, according to Wakefield Council.

The 110-room hotel was also expected to boost tourism and create new jobs, with developers saying it was expected to open its doors to customers by winter 2028.

A council spokesperson said: "We want to give people the opportunity to stay for longer and enjoy everything Wakefield has to offer - that's great news for our businesses and the local economy."

The new hotel, to be built by ION Property Developments Limited, would also receive £8m in government support from the Local Regeneration Fund to make the scheme "financially deliverable", the council said.

Its proximity to the East Coast Main Line - with short journey times to Leeds - was also expected to attract business stays to Wakefield, the spokesperson said.

Matthew Pinder, cabinet member for district regeneration and regional growth, said: "This is a big step forward for our city's growth."

articles.title: Brighton professor's research shows history of children's photos
articles.summary: A four-year study of children's photographs over the generations and archive material go on display.
articles.body:
The history of photographs taken by children has been revealed at a new exhibition.

University of Brighton researcher Annebella Pollen curated Snap Happy!, which opens at The Photographers' Gallery in London on Wednesday.

The show and an accompanying book were informed by the visual and material culture professor's four-year study of children's photographs over the generations.

"They may seem inconsequential, they may seem juvenile, foolish, amateurish, but I wanted to look at them closely and to take them seriously," Pollen told the BBC.

She said she had found examples of children's photography "from the late Victorian era right up to the present day".

The researcher added: "Photography was long something that was promoted only to boys but I discovered through looking at a lot of girls story papers, girls comics that these girl photographer figures appear."

Pollen's research explored what children snapped pictures of when they first get behind the camera and what their images tell us about childhood and creativity.

She had previously studied amateur photography and how cameras evolved from specialist equipment into a mass form of visual communication, according to the university.

Her book Whippersnappers: How Children Became Photographers traces the photography from school clubs in the 1880s, through to radical 1970s workshops and on to the digital age.

The exhibition, which runs until 21 February, includes moving images not featured in the book.

The archive collection on display includes advertising, manuals, comics and toys, as well as pictures taken of family, friends and pets as school projects or for experimentation.

Clare Grafik, curator at The Photographers' Gallery, said there was "something very attractive" to children about the analogue process and "a lot of young people are now re-engaging with analogue photography".

articles.title: Museum marks 60 years celebrating Oxfordshire's heritage
articles.summary: The Oxfordshire Museum in Woodstock will celebrate its diamond jubilee at a special event on Thursday.
articles.body:
A museum that showcases the history of Oxfordshire and its people is celebrating its 60th birthday this week.

The Oxfordshire Museum in Woodstock displays treasures dating as far back as the Roman occupation of Britain all the way to artefacts to the 20th Century.

On Thursday, the museum that first opened in 1966 will celebrate its diamond jubilee with a special event tracing its own story over the past six decades.

Jemma Davey, the museum service manager, said 60 years of "serving our residents and looking after the county's heritage is a really special thing".

"Although we're based in Woodstock, we are here to tell the story of Oxfordshire's people and place, and we go all the way back through to the Jurassic era, all the way through to contemporary objects and art that are made in the county," she said.

"We are very much here for the county and here for our residents."

To mark the anniversary, Thursday's event will celebrate "the museum, past, present and future", Oxfordshire County Council, which runs the site, said.

It will see Davey give a talk about the history of the museum itself, using archives from its own collection.

A special film, which sees visitors, staff and volunteers all share their memories and hopes for the museum, will also be screened.

"I was really conscious that this is not just a story for kind of one person to tell," Davey said.

"This is a story of so many people who have visited us, supported us, bought things in our cafe, visited our collections throughout the years."

Thursday's free celebration begins at 13:30 BST, and places must be booked in advance.

articles.title: Shropshire heating oil users face tough choices as prices rise
articles.summary: It comes as ministers say they will tighten up rules on heating oil and promote competition
articles.body:
With the summer gone and the central heating going on, people who use heating oil in their homes are facing the prospect of filling their tanks, at much higher prices than they have been used to.

Many will pay nearly double what they had to last year because of a rise in prices since the start of the Iran war.

It has led people like Liz Humphris, from Bishop's Castle in Shropshire, to limit how much they buy at once to help ends meet. "Now, I just order 500 litres at a time because it costs too much," she said.

Minimum order levels, set for some customers, will be reviewed.

As prices remain volatile, but significantly higher than in recent winters, campaigners have called for heating oil customers to benefit from a similar cap to that on mains gas and electricity tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales.

There is no promise this will happen, but ministers said they would work to "develop a regulatory regime for the heating oil market, protecting consumers and promoting competition."

Humphris said she had noticed the jump in prices: "It is costing over £500 for 500 litres, so it has gone up hugely."

Humphris added that she felt for people she knew who had to use food banks, like the one she volunteers for.

"I am reasonably OK because I've got a teacher's pension, so I am not destitute or anything," she said.

"For people who are on a very fixed income, it literally is coming down to the point where it is fuel or food, which is awful because you've got to heat your home."

According to Shropshire Council, about 15 per cent of households in its area rely on oil-fuelled central heating, which is between 16,000 and 21,000 properties.

But within the county there are large variations, with the South Shropshire constituency having one of the highest percentages of homes without mains gas across the UK, at 53%.

It has led to co-operatives forming to bulk buy heating oil at cheaper prices, including one set up by the charity Community Resource.

Hanna Clarke, who is the fundraising lead at the charity, said people coming to them were struggling with rising prices.

"It is different to your electricty and your gas. You can't necessarily put it on a direct debit and spread that cost out across the 12 months - you have to fill up your tank," she said.

"To be able to do it, lots of the suppliers have minimum orders, so that is the one sort of key issue that we are having, that they just literally cannot afford that big increase in the cost per unit now."

Campaign group Action with Communities in Rural England (ACRE) said the government's move to regulate the heating oil market did not go far enough.

Chief executive Corrine Pluchino called for an immediate cut to VAT on heating oil and LPG.

"While we welcome the government's announcement that they intend to accept the recommendations of the Competition and Markets Authority's study of the heating oil market, we do not believe the action will address the fundamental problem facing the 1.7 million UK households who are off the gas grid, mostly in rural areas," Pluchino added.

"For those households, especially those nearing the end of their current supply, the real issue is the high and volatile price of heating oil, which is adding hundreds of pounds to their bills because the fuel has to be bought in bulk."

articles.title: Plans for a large combined authority for the region are stalling
articles.summary: Why the "popular kids" in Oxfordshire are not letting Swindon in on the Thames Valley devolution deal.
articles.body:
If you have ever been picked last for a sports team, or not invited to a party, you might know how the Borough of Swindon feels right now.

The government wants district and borough councils to be scrapped to make way for larger combined authorities, many of which will be run by mayors.

The issue for Swindon, however, is that some of the council leaders in Berkshire and Oxfordshire do not want Swindon to join them in a Thames Valley authority, arguing the geography does not work.

Swindon Borough Council leader Gary Sumner said: "It's like not being invited to the party with the popular kids."

The leader of Oxfordshire County Council Tim Bearder said: "With no offence to my friends in Wiltshire, you are not in the Thames Valley."

The government wants most areas of England to be under a mayoral authority, promising each area a greater say on how money should be spent as well as more power to unlock growth.

Under current plans Swindon would be included in the Thames Valley, which Sumner said would be good for the region.

"Swindon is a vast economic powerhouse in a potential Thames Valley devolution deal," he said.

"This is about coming together for growth we can pitch for infrastructure funds that can unlock investment in our town centre."

Plan for £303m bypass dropped by government

Work to turn derelict site into museum set to begin

Plan for 2,000 EV charging points gets green light

Conservative Sumner also said Swindon could help rural Oxfordshire councils reach a housing target under spatial development strategy by agreeing to allocate more land for housing in the town centre.

"Oxfordshire don't want their green fields covered in houses," he said.

"We've got brownfield sites that could deliver thousands and thousands of homes, at pace".

However, Bearder said: "It is not something you can use as a bargaining chip to get into a Mayoral authority."

Plans are stalling , with some council leaders arguing against Swindon being involved.

"Perhaps they don't like the cut of Swindon's jib," said Sumner. "Perhaps they think they're too good for us.

"I'm really proud of our town and I'm upset when people think less of us and that's how it feels with two ends of the Thames Valley."

Windsor and Maidenhead council leaders also objected to the most recent plans, partly on the basis that a Foundation Strategic Authority was being proposed, instead of one run by a Mayor .

But on Swindon, Liberal Democrat Bearder said: "I don't think its a good fit. You would have to rearrange all the boundaries."

It is hoped under combined authorities, mayor and deputy mayors would also oversee things like the police and fire services - but currently Swindon's services operate in Wiltshire.

"It makes sense to have the set-up with Swindon staying in Wiltshire," Bearder said.

Meanwhile, Wiltshire Council leaders are looking to form a Wessex Mayoral Authority with nearby Somerset, Dorset and Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole.

Some leaders across Oxfordshire and Berkshire are keen on Swindon being involved.

Labour leader of Oxford City Council Susan Brown said it was "vital" Swindon was part of the Thames Valley.

"We're incredibly closely connected in terms of our economies," she said.

For a plan to be submitted to government, it needs approval from all parties across affected councils.

"It has to be unanimous and I will only do that when it is right," said Bearder.

Councils are waiting to hear what the next steps will be but elsewhere in the country local government reorganisation has been paused .

Sumner said he would continue to make the case for Swindon, hoping other leaders will have a change of heart.

"We need the Prime Minister to say, "If you want to see it happen, welcome Swindon," he said.

"This is the only thing that is going to get it across the line."

There are also discussions about whether or not Buckinghamshire and Milton Keynes would be part of the same group.

articles.title: Russia detains Japanese journalist on suspicion of spying
articles.summary: Russia’s FSB security agency said on Tuesday it had detained a Japanese journalist for alleged espionage, and Moscow’s Foreign Ministry said it regretted that Tokyo was using correspondents to carry out spying.
articles.body: Russia’s FSB security agency said on Tuesday it had detained a Japanese journalist for alleged espionage, and Moscow’s Foreign Ministry said it regretted that Tokyo was using correspondents to carry out spying. In a statement on its website, the FSB said the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper journalist was detained in the far eastern Sakhalin region on the day before he planned to leave Russia. It did not specify when this was. Russia and Japan, which never signed a formal World War Two peace treaty, have seen their diplomatic relations deteriorate since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, though Japan relies on Russia for supplies of liquefied natural gas (LNG). In a statement, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova identified the journalist as Imai Yuki, according to the Russian transliteration of his name, and said his detention cast a new pall on relations with Tokyo. Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said on Wednesday that Japan’s embassy in Moscow and consulate-general in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk had asked Russian authorities for information and called for fair treatment and humanitarian consideration for the Japanese national. Motegi did not confirm the identity of the person detained. The Hokkaido Shimbun said it was still confirming the details. “We will respond with the reporter’s safety as our top priority,” a spokesperson for the publisher said, declining to comment further. In a Russian state TV video report on the case, three masked men in black uniforms handcuffed a man lying on the ground as a voice off camera said he was suspected of spying. The video showed the man being accompanied by two FSB servicemen onto a plane, then in a cage in a Moscow court, which ordered him detained for nearly two months. The agency “thwarted the illegal activity” of the journalist, the FSB said. “As a result of intelligence operations, it was established that he gathered and stored information related to the country’s defense capabilities in order to pass it on for national intelligence purposes to be used against the security of the Russian Federation,” the statement said. “Tokyo’s attempts to use its correspondents in Russia with the status of foreign journalists to gather information for undermining our state’s security are regrettable,” the foreign ministry spokeswoman said. Japan, she said, had adopted an anti-Russian position during Russia’s military campaign in Ukraine and refused to consider Moscow’s concerns about Tokyo’s “remilitarization.” “We have to note that what has occurred will become an additional factor clouding the atmosphere of Russian-Japanese relations,” Zakharova said. Long-running disputes Russia regards Japan as an “unfriendly” country because it joined Western sanctions against Moscow over the war in Ukraine. Russia and Japan have a territorial dispute over the Kuril Islands, known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Russian President Vladimir Putin visited one of the disputed islands in August, causing uproar in Japan. A delegation from China’s Heilongjiang province also visited the island on Tuesday, amid strained relations between Beijing and Tokyo. Japan has said it would continue implementing sanctions against Russia and supporting Ukraine. This month, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s Cabinet approved additional sanctions against Russia, including expanded export bans and asset freezes targeting individuals affiliated with the Russian military. Asked whether improving US-Russia relations and Japan’s reliance on energy imports from Russia made it difficult for Tokyo to take countermeasures, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said: “It is true that there are many issues between Japan and Russia. “From Japan’s perspective, despite the difficult situation in Japan-Russia relations, Japan has taken resolute measures based on its position. At the same time, Russia is a neighboring country to Japan, and communication is necessary to resolve these issues.” One of the most prominent cases of a foreign journalist arrested in Russia was the detention of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich in 2023. He was found guilty of espionage by a Russian court, sentenced to 16 years and then freed in an East-West prisoner swap in August 2024.

articles.title: From Cairo to Tokyo: Can you guess these twin cities?
articles.summary: As a London borough moves to cut ties with Haifa, test your knowledge of the world’s twin cities.
articles.body:
Hackney, a borough in east London, is consulting residents until October 14 on whether to end its twinning with Haifa, Israel’s third-largest city, a link that dates back to 1968.

The Green Party-led council voted on July 28 to end the partnership in principle, citing its values and human rights commitments amid Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. Councillors will make a final decision after the consultation and a review of the borough’s twinning policy.

Twin cities, also called sister cities, are places in different countries linked by formal friendship agreements. These relationships can support school exchanges, cultural events and civic visits, though many become inactive over time.

Can you guess which cities are twinned? Take our quiz below.

Modern town twinning grew after World War II as a way to rebuild trust and foster peace. Coventry and Stalingrad (now Volgograd), both heavily bombed during the war, established a friendship link in 1944, often cited as the first modern city-twinning relationship.

The US city of St Paul and Japan’s Nagasaki established a sister-city partnership in 1955 to promote reconciliation after the atomic bombing of the latter in 1945. Cities have since formed links because of shared histories, similar roles as capitals or ports, or communities with roots in both places.

Because twinning is often symbolic, ending a link can allow a council to make a statement. Several UK councils suspended or ended links with Russian cities after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Prague’s relationship with Beijing also ended in 2019 amid a dispute involving Taiwan, after which the Czech Republic established a partnership with Taipei. Hackney’s proposal is the latest example of cities reassessing their international ties.
