articles.title: Sudan cannot afford to dismiss a chance for dialogue
articles.summary: A new initiative faces serious questions about military influence, but its critics should not write it off prematurely.
articles.body:
More than three years into the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Sudan is desperately in need of a political settlement. The fighting has caused immense suffering, and a military solution alone cannot rebuild the state or reunify its fractured society. Under such circumstances, any effort aimed at encouraging Sudanese-Sudanese dialogue deserves serious consideration rather than outright rejection.

In August, a self-appointed committee of 19 Sudanese public figures, chaired by Ahfad University President Qasim Badri, launched an initiative to prepare the ground for national dialogue inside Sudan. Its members had earlier met SAF chief General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and called for legal restrictions on opposition politicians to be lifted. The authorities subsequently issued a decree to drop certain politically motivated charges against Sudanese abroad returning for dialogue and grant participants temporary legal protections. These are limited but important confidence-building measures.

The initiative has nevertheless faced strong opposition. The civilian coalition Sumoud, led by former Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok, and Ta’sis, an alliance that includes the RSF, have opposed the proposed internal dialogue. They question its independence and warn that holding talks in army-controlled areas could legitimise al-Burhan’s authority and entrench the country’s divisions. These concerns are legitimate and deserve serious attention. But the committee says it is not seeking to negotiate Sudan’s future or determine the agenda of a national dialogue. Its role is to help create the conditions for Sudanese political actors to engage one another directly. The question is whether it can fulfil that role without allowing one side of the conflict to dominate the process. Dismissing the initiative before it has had an opportunity to demonstrate its value would be premature.

The country’s political actors and civil society organisations remain deeply divided, previous mediation efforts have faltered, and the war continues to make comprehensive political engagement increasingly difficult. The committee’s initiative is an attempt to break the deadlock. Efforts to prepare for political dialogue should not be postponed until the fighting stops. Securing a ceasefire and ensuring humanitarian access are urgent priorities, but preparations for political dialogue can proceed alongside efforts to achieve them.

The committee’s members were not elected, and they do not represent every political constituency. Yet the committee’s legitimacy cannot be judged solely by how it was created. It must also be judged by whether it can help bring a broader range of political actors into a national dialogue.

Good intentions alone cannot resolve concerns about credibility. Political dialogue can succeed only if participants believe the process is fair and independent. The legitimacy required to facilitate a political opening is not necessarily the same as that required to negotiate a national settlement. But even a preparatory initiative must earn the trust of those it seeks to bring together.

The committee’s meeting with al-Burhan was a practical necessity. As army chief and head of the Sovereignty Council, he was in a position to respond to the committee’s demands for legal protections. Engaging with al-Burhan does not in itself amount to an endorsement of his authority. But if the initiative becomes too closely associated with the army, other political actors may view it as an extension of al-Burhan’s political agenda rather than an independent facilitator. The committee must therefore demonstrate that its engagement extends beyond the military authorities and that it is prepared to work with political forces that oppose them.

The initiative was launched in Khartoum, which is under army control. This raises a genuine concern about whether a process beginning in territory controlled by one side of the war can attract the confidence of political forces across the country. A national dialogue cannot be confined to one geographical or political constituency. Entire regions have experienced different realities of war, governance, displacement and insecurity. The committee must find ways to reach those living outside army-controlled areas, including Sudanese displaced by the fighting, and ensure they can participate freely and without intimidation.

Sumoud and Ta’sis’s decision to reject the initiative does not automatically invalidate the process. Their concerns deserve consideration, but outright rejection at this early stage risks closing off an opportunity for political engagement. At the same time, their absence matters. Sudan’s crisis is too deep and complex to be addressed by any single political current. The committee cannot expect every stakeholder to endorse its initiative immediately, but it must create conditions that persuade reluctant actors to participate. If it fails to do so, the initiative itself will have failed.

The African Union Commission and the Arab League have also welcomed the initiative, providing an important measure of regional support. Their endorsement lends weight to the effort to revive Sudanese-led political dialogue, although external backing cannot substitute for the confidence of Sudan’s own political forces.

The committee’s initiative should therefore be judged without excessive optimism or automatic suspicion. The legal measures announced following its engagement with al-Burhan are an encouraging first step, but the real test lies ahead. Does it help remove legal and political obstacles facing opposition actors in practice, not just on paper? Can it win the confidence of those who have rejected it? Can it ensure that Sudanese across the country’s political and geographical divides have an opportunity to participate freely?

What is clear, however, is that Sudan’s crisis will ultimately require Sudanese actors with profoundly different visions of the country’s future to sit together and engage one another politically. No committee can do that on their behalf. No external actor can do it for them. At best, a preparatory initiative can help create the conditions under which such engagement becomes possible. The concerns raised by its critics should not be dismissed, but neither should they be grounds for rejecting the initiative before it has had an opportunity to address them. Those who have rejected it should remain open to reconsidering their position if the committee demonstrates that it can build an independent and inclusive process. If it succeeds, it will have rendered an important national service.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Bomb threat in Air India Frankfurt-Delhi flight: Pilot pressed hijack code; plane diverted to Jaipur
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: An Air India flight from Frankfurt to Delhi was diverted to Jaipur on Wednesday following a security alert triggered by a suspected hijack
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An Air India flight from Frankfurt to Delhi was diverted to Jaipur on Wednesday following a security alert triggered by a suspected hijack threat.The flight, AI-2030, landed safely and was immediately escorted to a designated isolation bay, adhering strictly to standard operating procedures for aviation security emergencies.Assistant Commissioner of Police (Malviya Nagar) Shiv Dayal said airport authorities had alerted the police about the emergency landing following the threat, news agency PTI reported.Police and security personnel were checking the aircraft in the isolation bay, he added.Pilot reportedly used hijack alert codeAccording to preliminary information, the pilot activated Squawk Code 7500, the internationally recognised transponder code indicating hijacking or unlawful interference, while the aircraft was in the Mumbai Flight Information Region (FIR).The aircraft was subsequently diverted to Jaipur, the source said. The number of passengers on board was not immediately known.Following the aircraft's safe landing, the pilots and passengers were deboarded in a phased manner under security supervision, according to the information available. Passengers and their baggage were undergoing security screening.Ground teams from the Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS), airport security agencies and local police cordoned off the isolation bay and began checking the aircraft.The National Security Guard (NSG) was also placed on standby in New Delhi, according to the information provided. Further details about the security alert and the ongoing investigation were awaited.In a similar incident in August, an Air India Express flight from Dammam, Saudi Arabia, to Delhi made an emergency landing at Ahmedabad airport after a tissue paper bearing the word “bomb” was found in the aircraft’s lavatory.All 32 passengers on board were safely deboarded at Terminal 2, according to Ahmedabad Police.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Indonesia relocates 8 orangutans into protected forest after rescue from wildfires
articles.summary: Eight endangered orangutans were released into a protected forest weeks after wildfires destroyed large swaths of their habitat in Indonesian Borneo, a conservation group said.
articles.body: JAKARTA, Indonesia — Eight endangered orangutans were released into a protected forest weeks after wildfires destroyed large swaths of their habitat in Indonesian Borneo, a conservation group said. The orangutans, including three mothers with infants and two adolescent males, were rescued from areas in Ketapang and North Kayong regencies that were ravaged by fires between August and September. The animals were moved Oct. 8 to Batu Nyambu protected forest in West Kalimantan province, said Heribertus Suciadi, a spokesperson for the Indonesian Nature Rehabilitation Initiative Foundation, or YIARI. The wildfires cut off habitat corridors and reduced access to food sources, forcing the apes into plantations inhabited by people in search of food and shelter and stranding them there, Suciadi told The Associated Press on Monday. “They had no burns, open wounds, broken bones or other life-threatening injuries, but appeared to be suffering from malnutrition and dehydration,” Suciadi said. Among those rescued were a female orangutan known as Mama Man and her infant, Man, who had been monitored for months in a small forest patch surrounded by plantations. Expanding fires and heavy smoke left them with no safe route back to larger forests before they were evacuated in early September, Suciadi said. Two other mother-and-infant pairs and two juvenile males were found in similar conditions after fires swept through forests near villages in Ketapang and North Kayong, Suciadi said. The orangutans underwent veterinary examinations and observation at a rehabilitation center operated by YIARI to ensure they were healthy enough to return to the wild. The release site in Batu Nyambu was selected because the area remains largely intact despite wildfires and offers abundant food sources, water, nesting trees and connections to neighboring forests, YIARI Operational Director Argitoe Ranting said before their release. “We want to ensure that rescued orangutans are not simply moved from one place to another, but actually have a chance to survive in their natural habitat,” he said, adding that protected forests capable of receiving displaced orangutans are becoming increasingly scarce as fires spread. Forest and land fires in Indonesia have worsened this year as El Niño intensifies a prolonged dry season. Contributing factors also include land clearances using fire in the Indonesian part of Borneo and regions of Sumatra island, as well as water shortages that have hampered Indonesian firefighters, who have received assistance from Japan. A male orangutan named Sampurna, believed to be around 20 years old, was found struggling to breathe by residents in early September on a palm oil plantation in West Kalimantan’s Ketapang district, an area affected by wildfires. He died hours after being rescued, Indonesia’s Forestry Ministry said. As of Saturday, the ministry said, more than 270 wild animals in Indonesia’s part of Borneo had been rescued, rehabilitated or guided to safer habitats, including 46 orangutans rescued by YIARI. The relocation was a last resort after the orangutans’ original habitat was no longer safe, YIARI CEO Karmele Llano Sanchez said. “These orangutans have been traumatized and other impacts by wildfires that devastated their habitat, leaving them displaced,” she said, “Rescuing them is one of the best ways we can help them survive.”

articles.body: American singer Mary Millben has alleged that US-based donors opposed to Prime Minister Narendra Modi are funding Abhijeet Dipke and the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), claiming that the money is being used to support forces seeking to disrupt governance in India.In a post on X, Millben appealed to young Indians to speak out, saying, “This is not the time to be silent.” She alleged that donors in the US opposed to PM Modi were funding individuals working against the prime minister and his leadership.Millben, known for her patriotic performances, came into the spotlight in India during the country's 75th Independence Day celebrations in 2022. She added, “There should always be a counter movement to uphold democracy and freedom,” before concluding her appeal with, “Rise up, young patriots! Rise up!”The allegations come amid questions raised by BJP leaders over the funding of CJP and its founder, Abhijeet Dipke. BJP president Nitin Nabin accused opposition leaders and the CJP of attempting to destabilise India with foreign backing, while BJP MP Nishikant Dubey questioned the sources of funding behind Dipke.Dipke has rejected allegations of foreign funding, arguing that if overseas money had entered the CJP's activities, it would amount to a failure of the Union home ministry. articles.title: AS Roma’s seven-game unbeaten streak poses fresh challenge for Real Madrid
articles.summary: Real Madrid face a difficult Champions League challenge against Roma on their visit to the Stadio Olimpico.Piero Gasperini’s side have developed into one of...
articles.body:
Real Madrid face a difficult Champions League challenge against Roma on their visit to the Stadio Olimpico.

Piero Gasperini's side have developed into one of Europe's most organised teams and are unbeaten in their opening seven matches of the season.

Roma's impressive start reflects the progress made under their manager, whose demanding approach has blended very well with the squad.

Roma's impressive numbers underline the threat

The Italian side have scored 14 goals and conceded just three this season, giving them the best goal difference in Serie A.

Their defensive success has been built around Gasperini's preferred three-man back line, supported by aggressive pressing and coordinated movement across the pitch.

Rather than abandoning the tactical principles that made him famous at Atalanta, the manager has assembled a squad suited to his methods.

Gasperini's Roma are one of the most in-form teams in Europe. (Photo by Valerio Pennicino/Getty Images)

Donyell Malen, in particular, has emerged as a dangerous attacking star, scoring six goals in six Serie A appearances.

Meanwhile, Paulo Dybala provides the technical quality and creativity needed to unlock opposition defences.

Why Roma could trouble Mourinho's Madrid

Roma's tactical structure presents an interesting challenge for Jose Mourinho, particularly given Madrid's recent difficulties progressing the ball through midfield.

Gasperini's aggressive man-oriented pressing could disrupt Madrid's build-up, forcing defenders into hurried passes and isolating their attacking players.

The midfield pairing of Federico Valverde and Aurelien Tchouameni will need to offer better passing options than they managed against Villarreal.

Mourinho could choose to play Bernardo Silva instead of one of the duo to help aid in the creativity against the Italian club.

Madrid could start Bernardo Silva to help with the midfield creativity. (Photo by Florencia Tan Jun/Getty Images)

However, Roma's commitment to the press could also present opportunities. The wing-backs are often caught high up the pitch.

This could potentially leave space for the wingers and Kylian Mbappe to exploit on the counter-attack.

Madrid must exploit Roma's biggest tactical risk

The key for Madrid could be resisting the temptation to attack too quickly whenever possession is recovered.

Against a well-drilled three-man defence, predictable long balls may simply surrender possession and allow Roma to regain control.

Instead, Mourinho's side should look to draw Roma's press forward before switching play into the spaces behind their wing-backs.

Arda Guler's ability to receive between the lines could be particularly useful in creating those opportunities.

Roma's unbeaten record shows that they deserve respect and will not be easy to get past, and Madrid will have to play a perfect game.

However, Mourinho has the quality on paper to do just that, and it remains to be seen how Los Blancos fare against the Italians.

articles.title: Russia batters Ukraine’s energy facilities hours after Zelensky appeals for early warnings from partners
articles.summary: A massive Russian attack on Ukrainian energy infrastructure left more than 600,000 people without power early Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, hours after warning his country had received no advance notice from Kyiv’s partners of a previous deadly round of strikes.
articles.body: A massive Russian attack on Ukrainian energy infrastructure left more than 600,000 people without power early Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, hours after warning his country had received no advance notice from Kyiv’s partners of a previous deadly round of strikes. Russia launched more than 120 drones and 39 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and Kharkiv, specifically targeting energy facilities, said Zelensky – causing widespread power outages and “significant damage” to oil and gas facilities. These are “the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President,” he wrote, referring to the “energy ceasefire” that President Donald Trump announced last weekend. CNN journalists in the capital reported hearing multiple explosions. Russia’s defense ministry also said it had downed 902 drones overnight, according to Russian news agency Interfax. Just hours earlier, Zelensky said his government had received “no early warning from our partners” before a deadly ballistic missile attack hit a major power plant in Kyiv and damaged a residential building on Tuesday. Ukraine’s air defenses had “detected these missiles only when they were already virtually on approach to Kyiv,” he said. “This is absolutely unjust: when they (Russia) are destroying our energy infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches.” Intelligence provided by the US and other partners helps Ukraine defend against Russian ballistic missile attacks by providing the locations of missile launchers as well as data on where the strikes are heading, and when. The strikes come after the Trump administration warned Ukraine and allies in Europe last weekend that the US could suspend intelligence sharing and European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine if Kyiv does not halt its deep strikes on Russian energy facilities. However, when asked Tuesday, Trump said the US had not stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine. “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end, so we’re working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end,” he said. The sharing is no guarantee of protection. Russia’s ballistic missiles can reach Kyiv in just minutes, leaving little time to respond; in some recent attacks, air raid sirens sounded at the same time as the first explosions. For months, Zelensky has urged partners to help bolster Ukraine’s air defenses, especially in providing more ballistic-missile interceptors – one of the few weapons capable of knocking down ballistic missiles that travel faster than the speed of sound. Trump had announced the so-called energy ceasefire on Sunday, which appeared to take both warring countries by surprise. Afterward, Zelensky said he supported the ceasefire even though he did not know about it in advance. The Kremlin has not commented directly on it. By Monday, Zelensky said Russia had already violated the supposed ceasefire with fresh strikes – but said he was willing to abide by the agreement if Moscow does too. When asked by reporters on Tuesday whether Russia had violated the ceasefire, Trump said: “I’ll let you know about that later,” according to Reuters. Russia and Ukraine have ramped up their attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure in recent months, as front lines on the ground stay largely unmoved.

articles.title: ‘Like we don’t exist’: Palestinians in West Bank denied say in Israel vote
articles.summary: Palestinians in the occupied West Bank see little prospect Israel’s election will change their lives under occupation.
articles.body:
Jabal al-Baba, occupied West Bank – In Jabal al-Baba, a small Bedouin community east of Jerusalem, Israel controls almost every aspect of Palestinians’ daily life, from building homes and accessing water to moving freely.

Yet when Israelis head to the polls on October 27, the vast majority of the nearly three million Palestinians in the occupied West Bank will have no say in choosing the government that rules their lives under occupation – unlike the 700,000 Jewish settlers living in some 300 illegal settlements and outposts across the territory, including occupied East Jerusalem.

“They treat us like something that doesn’t exist,” said Atallah al-Jahalin, Jabal al-Baba’s community representative.

“You don’t have the right to vote. You don’t have the rights that you would have in a democratic state.”

About 450 people live in Jabal al-Baba, a community in Area C, which makes up about 60 percent of the occupied West Bank and remains under full Israeli military and civil control.

Many residents here raise sheep and goats beside homes made from corrugated metal. Most belong to the Jahalin tribe, whose families were expelled from the Naqab (Negev) desert region by Israeli authorities in the years after the Nakba, the violent ethnic cleansing of Palestine by Zionist militias in 1948.

“You are forbidden from building a house. You are forbidden from building a street. You are forbidden from building a school,” said al-Jahalin. “Everything is forbidden to us.”

Residents face constant pressure from Israeli soldiers and settlers, al-Jahalin said, on top of repeated demolitions.

“In the past few years, we have had more than 100 demolition operations in our community,” he said. “We were constantly rebuilding our homes.”

Israel says it demolishes Palestinian structures built without permits , which are almost impossible for Palestinians to obtain. Israeli rights group Bimkom found authorities rejected more than 99 percent of Palestinian building permit applications in Area C between 2021 and 2024.

While Palestinians are restricted from developing, Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law, are expanding at a record pace. In April, Israel’s security cabinet was reported to have approved 34 new settlements in a single decision, including outposts legalised retroactively, according to Peace Now, an Israeli anti-settlement watchdog group.

For al-Jahalin, the aim is clear: to push his community out and make way for settlers.

“There is an Israeli plan to displace the people who are here,” he said. “All of this is a means of pressure. We have to leave these areas for the benefit of the settlement projects.”

In this month’s vote, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud Party and the far-right coalition it leads face a tight race against an opposition alliance consisting of an assortment of parties that are united in their stated aim to “preserve and strengthen Israel as a Jewish and democratic state”.

The opposition grouping has not declared an official leader, but former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, of the centrist Yashar party, is seen as its most likely candidate for prime minister.

Recent polls indicate the two blocs are running neck and neck, with neither side appearing on course to win a majority. Most leaders of the Jewish-led opposition bloc, meanwhile, have ruled out joining forces with the Arab-led parties that represent the Palestinian citizens of Israel who make up about 20 percent of its population.

But for many Palestinians, a change at the top would mean little .

Jamal Juma’, coordinator of the grassroots Stop the Wall campaign, said decades of occupation have taught Palestinians not to expect a new government to shift fundamental Israeli policies. He pointed out that it was Israel’s centre-left Labour Party – and not the right – that began building settlements in the West Bank after 1967.

For Jabal al-Baba, the clearest test of what a change in government would mean is E1, a strip of land between Jerusalem and the illegal settlement of Ma’ale Adumim, where the community sits.

The E1 project would link the settlement to Jerusalem, cutting the West Bank in two and threatening the forced displacement of some 18 Bedouin communities, including Jabal al-Baba.

In August 2025, Israel gave final approval to 3,401 settler homes in E1, which far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said would “bury” the idea of a Palestinian state . A month later, Netanyahu vowed “there will be no Palestinian state. This place belongs to us.”

This year, the government put the land up for sale in two tenders, timed to advance before the election. Israel’s attorney general has since moved to delay parts of the process until after the vote, and Smotrich is challenging that in court.

In the lead-up to the election, Eisenkot rejected the idea of a Palestinian state as “delusional” while also expressing support for “strengthening” settlements. But asked about the E1 tenders in August , he said: “Not now.” He called advancing the project a mistake with an international cost, and said far-right ministers and settler violence were damaging Israel’s standing abroad.

That puts him at odds with the current government over the timing of E1 – but not over the idea of settling the West Bank.

“There may be a democracy, but only for Jewish people,” said Kareem Jubran, field research director at Israeli rights group B’Tselem, which describes Israel’s rule over Palestinians as apartheid.

“Even if the governments change, the system remains,” he said. “If the left exists, it is a Zionist left. It is not very influential in Israeli political life.”

In Jabal al-Baba, where settlement expansion threatens the community’s future, al-Jahalin has reached a similar conclusion.

“It may be Eisenkot, it may be Netanyahu,” he said. “Israeli policy is already on the table. It doesn’t matter who carries it out.”

Whoever forms Israel’s next government will continue to exercise decisive power over the lives of Palestinians in the West Bank, which was divided into three areas – A, B and C – as part of the Oslo Accords in the 1990s.

Israel’s control is most direct in Area C, but its restrictions reach across the West Bank.

“The Israelis are controlling everything in the West Bank, every single thing,” said Juma’, of the Stop the Wall campaign, citing Israel’s control of the movement between Palestinian cities and villages, as well as access to water and electricity and the territory’s borders.

“Every city and every village, they have constructed a gate at the entrance,” he added.

Juma’ also warned that continued fragmentation could turn the West Bank into isolated enclaves, cutting Palestinian communities off from one another.

“It will be like open prisons, like Gaza,” he said. “But here we have different Gazas.”

Jubran, of B’Tselem, said stopping that trajectory depends on international pressure, not the outcome of Israel’s election.

“If the international community were determined to take practical steps to stop the E1 project, it could,” he said. “As long as it is not, E1 will go ahead.”

Back in Jabal al-Baba, the threat of renewed forcible displacement is looming large.

Al-Jahalin said his family was expelled from the Naqab once already – but he will not leave again.

“I am not ready to live the life of my father,” he said. “I, as a Palestinian, will stay, whether I die or live on this Earth.”

The illegal Israeli settlement of Ma’ale Adumim in the occupied West Bank, viewed from the Bedouin village of Jabal al-Baba, which faces the threat of forcible displacement as plans to expand settlements in the E1 area move forward [Leila Warah/Al Jazeera]
A campaign billboard for Israeli politician Gadi Eisenkot stands at the entrance to an Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank [Leila Warah/Al Jazeera]

articles.title: Russian strikes leave 600,000 without power in Ukraine, Zelensky says
articles.summary: Ukraine's president says "critical" infrastructure was hit overnight, while emergency services say at least three were killed.
articles.body:
At least 600,000 people across Ukraine are now without electricity after deadly overnight Russian missile and drone strikes, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

He said "critical" energy infrastructure had been hit in Kyiv and the capital region and also in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv - despite a claim by US President Donald Trump on Sunday that an "energy ceasefire" was in place between Russia and Ukraine.

In Kyiv, at least three people were killed and 21 injured, Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS said.

Russia's defence ministry said its "massive" strikes overnight had targeted communications and energy facilities in the Kyiv and Kharkiv regions used by Ukraine's military.

The defence ministry also said 902 Ukrainian drones had been shot down overnight over a number of Russian regions, including the capital Moscow and Crimea - Ukraine's southern peninsula annexed by Russia in 2014.

Ukraine's air force said that overnight, Russia had launched 39 ballistic and cruise missiles and 128 drones, and that four of those missiles and 115 drones had been shot down.

On Sunday, Trump wrote in a post on social media: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"

President Zelensky has since repeatedly said Ukraine is ready to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow did the same.

But Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. Under any truce, he added, Europe would be able to "pump [Ukraine] with new weapons" for it to continue the war.

Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

articles.title: Why Sri Lanka’s Rajapaksas are being investigated for corruption and crimes
articles.summary: Several members and allies of once-powerful dynasty, including the wife of ex-President Mahinda Rajapaksa, are under arrest.
articles.body:
Colombo, Sri Lanka – A court in the Sri Lankan capital has extended the custody of the wife of Sri Lanka’s powerful former President Mahinda Rajapaksa, who was arrested last week over allegations that her charity misused donations collected for a children’s hospital.

The October 7 arrest of Shiranthi Rajapaksa , 73, dealt a huge blow to the once powerful family that ruled Sri Lanka for nearly two decades until they were overthrown in a youth-led uprising in 2022.

A month before Shiranthi’s arrest, her 40-year-old parliamentarian son Namal Rajapaksa, who is also the national organiser of the Rajapaksa-controlled Sri Lanka Podujana Peramuna (SLPP) party, was arrested over bribery charges. He remains in custody.

The family, based in the stronghold of Hambantota district in southern Sri Lanka, counts Mahinda, 80, as its charismatic patriarch.

Elected prime minister in 2004 and president the next year, Mahinda is adored by many among the country’s majority ethnic Sinhala Buddhists for crushing the Tamil separatist rebels who waged a 26-year-long civil war that ended in 2009.

In the campaign against the now-defunct Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels demanding a separate state in northern Sri Lanka, Mahinda’s younger brother Gotabaya Rajapaksa served as his defence secretary.

According to estimates by the United Nations, nearly 40,000 civilians were killed in the final weeks of the civil war, triggering an international inquiry into the alleged atrocities. After the war, Mahinda was criticised for not doing enough to mend relations with the Tamils, who have been banned from commemorating their war dead.

During Mahinda’s rule, Sri Lanka, a country of 22 million people, also borrowed nearly $7bn from China for infrastructure projects, many of which were mired in corruption.

Despite changing a law that allowed him a third presidential term, Mahinda lost the 2015 election to former political ally, Maithripala Sirisena.

After the deadly 2019 Easter Sunday bombings in churches and hotels blamed on an ISIL (ISIS) offshoot, Gotabaya, who until then was a political novice, used anti-Muslim rhetoric to win the presidential election – the second in the family to hold the post.

Gotabaya appointed Mahinda as the prime minister, and gave influential ministerial posts to his other brothers – Chamal and Basil – as well as Mahinda’s son, Namal Rajapaksa.

As the family tightened its control over the island struck first by the 2019 bombings and later the coronavirus pandemic, they were also accused of mismanaging the economy and widespread corruption.

The economic crisis ignited historic street protests in the summer of 2022, which forced Gotabaya to flee the country. A caretaker government ruled the country until elections in 2024 saw Anura Kumara Dissanayake, a 57-year-old Marxist, winning the presidency on an anti-corruption platform and promising to act against the Rajapaksa family and previous administrations.

What are the corruption allegations against the family?

The ongoing arrests and legal cases against members of the Rajapaksa family are seen as a part of the same promise.

The former First Lady Shiranthi Rajapaksa was arrested last week by the government’s Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption (CIABOC).

The Siriliya Saviya foundation, a charity she leads, is accused of misusing donations of nearly 100m rupees ($30,000) intended to buy equipment for a children’s hospital in capital Colombo.

Investigators told a court that a MRI scanner had already been donated by the Chinese government, but the charity allegedly continued to solicit donations for a scanner and misused the funds.

Sagara Kariyawasam, the general secretary of Sri Lanka Podujana Peramuna (SLPP), the party led by the Rajapaksa family, denies the allegation.

“It is untrue and the money is safe in the frozen bank account of Siriliya Saviya,” he told Al Jazeera.

But CIABOC told the court their investigations revealed that the money was used to buy a house and that they would initiate steps to freeze the asset.

On Monday, her lawyers approached a court for anticipatory bail on health grounds. But the plea was rejected. On Tuesday, Shiranthi was presented before the court, which extended her custody until Friday.

Meanwhile, Mahinda’s son Namal is being tried in a case involving the alleged payment of a $30,000 bribe in a government deal with Airbus to buy planes for the national airline.

He faces another investigation where he is allegedly linked to a $211,000 bribe paid by a foreign private company to expedite a government land transfer.

Both incidents allegedly happened during his father’s presidency.

Mahinda’s other son Yoshitha, 38, is also being investigated for money laundering, while Shasheendra Rajapaksa, the 50-year-old son of Chamal Rajapaksa, is currently out on bail in connection with a corruption case.

Also, Basil, another Rajapaksa sibling, is facing an arrest warrant for failing to appear before court in a case related to purchasing properties allegedly using illicit money. He is believed to be in the United States.

Last week, the Financial Crimes Investigation Division seized Basil’s property in Matara, a southern coastal town.

What other charges does the family face?

But it’s not just corruption cases hounding the powerful family.

Gotabaya is barred from travelling abroad over allegations that the 2019 Easter Sunday bombings were staged to boost his popularity ahead of the 2019 presidential election.

Last week, a Sri Lankan court rejected his appeal to prevent his likely arrest in the ongoing investigation into the simultaneous bombings in three churches and three hotels, killing 279 people, 45 of them foreigners, in the worst such attack on the island popular for tourism.

In 2023, a whistleblower told the British network Channel 4 that former Sri Lankan intelligence chief Suresh Salley had met the alleged bombers behind the 2019 attacks, as part of a conspiracy to influence the upcoming election.

Gotabaya declared his candidacy two days after the attacks, and his campaign focused on combating “Islamic extremism”. Salley was arrested in February this year under terror laws and is being investigated over the Easter Sunday bombings.

Ramindu Perera, a researcher in international law at the European University Institute in Italy, says if the allegation that the Rajapaksas were connected to the 2019 attacks is proved, it would have a “devastating effect” on the family.

“Such revelations are likely to further delegitimise the SLPP’s standing in Sri Lankan politics,” he said. The party has been reduced to just three seats in the 225-member national parliament.

Last month, Sri Lanka’s High Court convicted 15 of the 24 Muslim men accused of involvement in the 2019 bombings, but families of many victims said they are still waiting for the “masterminds” to be held accountable.

How have Sri Lankans reacted to the investigations?

Addressing a public rally at Nikawerariya in northwestern Sri Lanka on Sunday, President Dissanayake said the law will be applied to everyone equally.

“Those who gained social power, political power and positional power, used those powers to be above the law. But, under this government, the law is equal for everyone,” he said.

“If anyone believes that the law will not reach them, we are now proving that there is no place where law cannot reach and no one is beyond its reach,” he added.

But SLPP’s Kariyawasam accused the government of misleading the people.

“We don’t have any problem with thieves being punished after proving their wrongdoings,” he told Al Jazeera.

“But the government is taking people to custody without any court trials, and then tells the people that they punish thieves. This is purely a political witch-hunt.”

Researcher Perera said the demand for accountability in corruption cases was the main slogan that brought Dissanayake to power.

“As action against corruption is at the core of the NPP government’s mandate, what is happening now should be seen as an attempt to enforce that mandate,” he told Al Jazeera, referring to Dissanayake’s National People’s Power party.

Political analyst Gamini Viyangoda also rejected Kariyawasam’s claim. “This is not a political witch-hunt, but implementing the rule of law.”

articles.title: Ex-DRC President Kabila’s alliance with M23 rebels: Why it matters
articles.summary: Kabila’s move confirms numerous accusations from the government in Kinshasa of his ties to armed rebels.
articles.body:
Former President Joseph Kabila of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has officially allied with armed rebel groups, raising fears of further escalation of an ongoing conflict in the country’s east that has already killed thousands.

Kabila on Monday launched a new political-military coalition to replace the M23-AFC alliance, which is fighting government forces and controls swaths of territory.

The new movement will “put an end to tyranny by any means necessary, including the use of force”, coalition spokesperson Claude Ibalanky said, in what appeared to be a chilling threat to the government in Kinshasa.

It comes precisely a year after Kabila was sentenced to death by a military court for alleged links to the rebel groups.

The M23 crisis has racked the mineral-rich eastern DRC for nearly 15 years. The United Nations says more than 7.8 million people are displaced while 28 million people face food shortages. An untold number have died.

The United States and UN accuse Rwanda of backing M23. Kigali denies it.

Kabila introduced the new alliance, the Front pour la Refondation de la Nation (FRN), from his residence in Goma, confirming the DRC government’s accusations.

The former president said he will lead the alliance.

Corneille Nangaa, a Kabila ally who served as a former elections commissioner before leaving government to launch the Congo River Alliance (AFC), will serve as deputy, alongside Bertrand Bisimwa, an M23 spokesman.

Freddy Kaniki, a medical doctor and senior M23 health official, will serve as secretary-general, while Sultani Makenga of the M23 will be the army chief of the alliance.

Kabila, 55, is the son of former President Laurent Kabila.

He took office as a 29-year-old back in 2001 after his father was assassinated. He previously served as army chief and fought in the two Congo civil wars , when Rwanda backed rebel groups against longtime Congolese leader Mobutu Sese Seko.

Kabila’s term, which officially ended in 2016, was marked by rights violations and corruption. He illegally delayed elections until 2018, citing voter registration challenges, and left office in 2019.

Before he stepped down, Kabila is believed to have signed a power-sharing deal with opposition candidate and election winner, current President Felix Tshisekedi. Kabila’s allies were initially installed throughout the cabinet after the deal, but in 2020, Tshisekedi began removing them, as their truce collapsed on a bitter note.

Tshisekedi’s government also launched corruption investigations against Kabila, forcing him into self-imposed exile in South Africa in 2023.

Why has Kabila joined the rebel alliance?

The former president’s latest move is unsurprising; Kinshasa has long alleged his ties to the M23-AFC alliance.

Amid intensifying M23-AFC offensives last year, Kabila wrote a scathing opinion piece in South Africa’s Sunday Times, accusing Tshisekedi of mishandling the conflict and proposing a “12-point plan” to restore peace. Reports also emerged of Kabila’s sighting in the eastern rebel-held Goma, where he owns homes.

Last October, a military court in Kinshasa sentenced Kabila to death on charges of treason, war crimes, and other major offences for alleged collaboration with Rwanda and M23-AFC.

In April, Washington imposed sanctions on Kabila, alleging that he funded rebel groups.

Eastern DRC has been engulfed in violence for more than 30 years, and multiple groups have been fighting to dominate the region. The roots of the crisis go back to the 1994 genocide in neighbouring Rwanda, the alleged harbouring of Hutu fighter groups in the DRC in its aftermath, Kigali’s determination to fight them, and deep-rooted tribalism.

The March 23 Movement (M23) emerged in 2012 from the remnants of Congolese Tutsi fighter groups that fought in the Second Congo War. It claims to be fighting for the rights of minority Congolese Tutsis and seeks to unseat the government in Kinshasa.

M23 first took Goma and other towns in the east in 2012 offensives; however, its fighters were pushed back by a special UN force fighting alongside the FARDC – the Congolese military.

In 2022, amid Tshisekedi’s fallout with Kabila, M23 resurfaced with renewed force, allegedly backed by more than 4,000 Rwandan soldiers. Kigali has long accused successive governments in Kinshasa of supporting the DRC-based Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) armed group, which includes Hutu genocidaires.

In 2023, as the M23 seized several towns and the Congolese army fell back, Nangaa, the then-elections commissioner, also fell out with Tshisekedi – reportedly over his move to run in elections. He then went into exile, formed the AFC, and allied with M23 as its political arm.

In early 2024, AFC-M23 launched lightning offensives that saw it sweep across vast swaths of the east, rapidly seizing territory. Goma fell again to the AFC-M23 in January 2025, following heavy battles that killed nearly 3,000 civilians.

The rebels, who have been accused of civilian massacres, currently hold North and South Kivu, where Kabila is from, including their capitals Goma and Bukavu, as well as border crossings with Rwanda and Uganda. Kampala has also been accused of supporting M23.

Al Jazeera’s Alain Uaykani reported that Congolese are worried the conflict could escalate again, and that a number of soldiers could defect to serve their former boss.

There are also fears that ongoing peace talks could collapse. In June 2025, DRC and Rwanda signed a US-led peace agreement.

In a separate process mediated by Qatar, the DRC and M23-AFC also signed the Doha Framework last November and were meant to meet this month.

But the changes may not end the agreements between the DRC and Rwanda, as Kigali will likely want to continue with the US-led talks, Bram Verelst of the Institute for Security Studies told Al Jazeera.

The real threat, he warned, lies to the Doha process.

“We are likely to see a hardening of Kinshasa’s position toward the rebel movement and Kabila, including efforts to isolate Kabila and FRN regionally,” Verelst noted.

“What this means for the conflict on the ground will depend on the capacity of Kabila to take control over the rebellion and to build and expand alliances beyond North and South Kivu,” he added.
